inequality.title: Empowering Women, Empowering Energy: The Role of Intra-household Bargaining Power in Alleviating Multidimensional Energy Poverty in Rural China
inequality.title_ja: 女性のエンパワーメントとエネルギー：中国農村部における多次元エネルギー貧困緩和に対する世帯内交渉力の役割
summary_ja: 2014-2020年の中国家庭パネル調査データを用い、農村女性の世帯内交渉力が多次元エネルギー貧困に与える影響を分析した。
世帯内交渉力の尺度が1単位上昇すると、多次元エネルギー貧困（MEP）の発生可能性が8.0%ポイント減少することが判明した。
媒介分析により、世帯所得の向上や非クリーンエネルギー利用の減少を経由してエネルギー貧困が緩和されることが示された。
inequality.reason_ja: 多次元貧困測定や世帯内不平等の実証に関心を持つ研究者に直接役立つため。
inequality.abstract: Improving women’s intra-household bargaining power (IHBP) and reducing energy poverty in rural areas contribute to achieving the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, such as achieving gender equality, empowering all women and girls (Goal 5), and ensuring access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all (Goal 7). This study explores the impact of rural women’s IHBP on multidimensional energy poverty (MEP), using data from the 2014-2020 China Family Panel Studies and a conditional mixed-process model. We construct a composite index to measure rural women’s IHBP, accounting for dimensions of asset ownership, labor allocation/labor market participation, household financial management, household expenditure allocation, and household decision-making power. Our results suggest that women’s IHBP is negatively and significantly associated with household MEP. A one-unit increase in rural women’s IHBP is associated with an 8.0-percentage-point reduction in the probability of household MEP. The negative association between women’s IHBP and MEP remains stable across male- and female-headed households, although the estimates for the two subgroups do not differ significantly. Meanwhile, all variables used to construct women’s IHBP are negatively and significantly associated with MEP. The mediation analysis suggests that women’s IHBP is associated with lower MEP incidence through increased household income and reduced use of non-clean energy. Our findings remind policymakers that they should pay more attention to empowering rural women in their efforts to reduce energy poverty.

inequality.title: Equal opportunities in school choice settings
inequality.title_ja: 学校選択制度における機会均等
summary_ja: 機会均等の概念を学校選択に導入し、生徒と学校のマッチングの質（マッチクオリティ）の分布に基づく新たな公平性を定義した。
安定性を前提条件とし、公平性と総マッチング品質による効率性を両立させる配分を考察し、概念間の不整合性を整理した。
定義を緩和した線形社会福祉関数を設定し、安定マッチング集合上で社会福祉を最大化するアルゴリズムを提案・適用した。
inequality.reason_ja: 機会均等の理論を実際の制度設計や政策の最適化へ応用する研究であるため。
inequality.abstract: We introduce a novel notion of fairness, inspired by the equality of opportunity literature, into the school choice setting, endowed with a measure of the match qualities between students and schools. In this framework, fairness considerations are made by a social evaluator based on the match quality distribution. We impose the standard notion of stability as a minimal desideratum and study matchings that satisfy our notion of fairness and an efficiency requirement based on aggregate match quality. To overcome some of the identified incompatibilities, we relax the fairness and efficiency definitions, and embed them in a family of linear social welfare functions. We then propose an algorithm that maximize social welfare over the set of stable matchings. Finally, we illustrate our approach with an application to the allocation of Italian high school students in the 2021/2022 academic year. JEL: C78, D63

inequality.title: The hidden Great Levelling that standard inequality measures miss
inequality.title_ja: 従来の不平等指標が見落とす隠された「大平準化」
summary_ja: 1820年以降の上位1%所得シェアは一律18%に見えるが、生存に必要な最低水準（生存床）が考慮されていない。
生存床を除いた余剰所得の分析では、上位1%の余剰シェアは1820年の53%から現在19%へと大幅に低下した。
下位50%の余剰シェアは1-3%から13%へ上昇しており、実質的自由を支える資源の不平等は改善している。
inequality.reason_ja: 生存制約を取り入れた新たな不平等測定手法と長期実証分析を把握できるため。
inequality.abstract: Have two centuries of economic and institutional change made societies more equal? By standard measures, the answer is no. Across the 48 countries with long-run data, the richest 1%’s share of national income averaged 18% in 1820. It is 18% today. Read at face value, these figures suggest organised labour, democratisation and decolonisation left elite control over resources unchanged. In this paper, Andrés Irarrázaval documents a global Great Levelling, invisible in standard top income shares. In poorer times, much of national income was tied to subsistence. Transferring this income to the top 1% would have left the other 99% below what they needed to survive. The paper factors this subsistence constraint into inequality measurement and studies how the surplus, income not tied to subsistence, is distributed within 48 countries over two centuries. KEY FINDINGS The top 1% share of national surplus fell from 53% in 1820 to 40% in 1920 and 19% today, a nearly threefold decline in elite control over transferable resources (Figure 1A). Top income shares hide this decline because they are measured against all national income, including the part needed for subsistence. The paper calls this part the subsistence floor. In 1820, that floor made up 62% of national income. Today it makes up 10% (Figure 1B). The same 18% of national income was therefore a much bigger slice of the surplus then than now. The new surplus went mainly to the other 99%. Growth, by lifting incomes above subsistence, expanded the share of national income that could accrue to the top 1%, from 38% in 1820 to 90% today. Yet top income shares did not rise over the long run. The bottom 50% were the main winners. Their average share of national surplus rose from 1–3% before the Second World War to 13% today. Surplus income gives households the means to pursue goals beyond immediate necessity, such as saving, affording leisure or paying for a child’s education. That capacity underpins what Amartya Sen (1999) calls “substantive freedoms”, and it is now far more widely shared. The Great Levelling began in the late 19th century, coinciding with the rise of organised labour and mass democracy (Figure 1A). It was steepest during and after the Second World War and partly reversed after 1980. Redistribution played a secondary role. Comparing pre-tax with post-tax surplus shares, the paper finds that taxes and transfers account for only a tenth of the long-run fall in the top 1% surplus share. The evidence points instead to pre-distribution forces that raised workers’ market incomes, such as their rising bargaining power. By the late 19th century, industrialisation had concentrated workers in factories. There they could organise, threaten unrest and press for a wage floor well above bare subsistence. Figure 1. The top 1% share of national income barely moved over two centuries, while its share of the surplus fell almost threefold (panel A), as growth lifted incomes far above the subsistence floor (panel B). Notes. The top 1% share of national surplus = (top 1% income share × national income − 1% × subsistence floor) / (national income − subsistence floor). The subsistence floor as a share of national income is the minimum cost of subsistence per capita over national income per capita. The world series is the country average weighted by population. See Irarrázaval, The Hidden Great Levelling, for details. AUTHOR Andrés Irarrázaval, London School of Economics The post The hidden Great Levelling that standard inequality measures miss appeared first on WID - World Inequality Database .

inequality.title: Locked out: Drivers and consequences of housing affordability pressures in Europe
inequality.title_ja: 締め出される人々：欧州における住宅手頃感圧力の要因と帰結
summary_ja: 欧州の住宅コスト上昇の要因は、世界金融危機前の金融供給から近年は供給制約へと変化している。

inequality.abstract: Rising housing costs have intensified affordability crises across Europe. This column examines the drivers of this growth, its distributional effects on households, and implications for labour mobility. While the pre-global financial crisis rise in house prices was largely driven by credit supply, housing supply constraints have become a more important driver of prices in recent years. Housing affordability pressures are highly uneven across location, housing tenure, income groups, and the level of urbanisation, and have widened income and wealth gaps between owners and renters. Beyond distributional concerns, declining affordability also has adverse consequences for labour allocation and efficiency.

Establishing an office of worker advocacy that would provide services to workers in a similar fashion to the support the U.S. Small Business Administration offers to small business owners and entrepreneurs. Enlisting social scientists to staff surge teams for a future administration that will need many new people on day one, scaling tools such as Intergovernmental Personnel Act assignments that have so far been ad hoc. Restoring the Presidential Management Fellows program at the White House Office of Personnel Management, a program terminated in 2025. What this means for growth: Social scientists have a clear role to play in ensuring that new government programs and policies are grounded in evidence and embed democratic participation that work toward a more equitable future. Overview The Washington Center for Equitable Growth earlier this month convened a panel of scholars and former senior officials at the Association for Public Policy Analysis and Management’s Fall Research Conference in Boston, titled “ Reimagining and Rebuilding Government: The Role of Social Scientists in Evidence-Backed Policymaking .” Held on November 6, our APPAM discussion explored how social scientists can help rebuild the capacity of the federal government and public trust in it at a moment when both are under severe strain. Opening the session, Korin Davis , Equitable Growth’s director of academic programs, described the dual tasks facing the field. Tens of thousands of civil servants have either left government or been pushed out, federal statistical agencies are being systematically weakened, and trust in government is low. Yet Davis framed the moment as an opportunity to reimagine what kind of government Americans want and to rebuild the workforce and institutions needed to deliver it. Linder Professor of Social Science and founding director of the Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab at the Institute for Advanced Study, opened the discussion by arguing that the founding assumption that scientific autonomy inherently serves the public interest has not been fully borne out and indeed no longer holds. Her central point: commitment to democratic participation and accountability cannot come second to reforming government. signals.title: Does AI have consciousness? Berggruen Prize-winning philosopher Thomas Nagel says no
signals.title_ja: AIに意識はあるか？ ベルグルエン賞受賞の哲学者トマス・ネーゲルは「ノー」と語る

signals.abstract: What is it like to be a bat? Philosopher Thomas Nagel posed that question in a seminal 1974 essay of the same name, arguing that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism – something it is like for the organism.” In other words, if there is a unique experience of being a human, and a unique experience of being a bat, then humans and bats are conscious. Nagel, 89, was born in Belgrade to Jewish refugee parents and raised in the US. He earned his doctorate at Harvard studying under John Rawls and spent his career at the University of California Berkeley, Princeton and New York University, where he has explored the question of consciousness and the so-called “mind-body problem”. He has just been awarded the $1m (€890,000) Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture. Here, Nagel speaks to Monocle from New York about the renewed relevance of his work in the age of AI . This conversation has been edited for clarity and length. (Image: Janet Malcolm/Courtesy of the Berggruen Institute) More than 50 years ago you wrote that robots can behave like people but experience nothing. Have you updated that assertion with the advent of artificial intelligence? It doesn’t require any updating because these devices are not serious candidates for the attribution of consciousness for two reasons. First, the physical basis of their operation has absolutely no resemblance to the physical substrate of consciousness in biological organisms. They operate on the basis of widely dispersed data systems and algorithms that pick sequences of sentences . Second, the physical output of large language models provides no evidence of consciousness because it is entirely linguistic. The only things that they produce are words – and language is not one of the natural manifestations of consciousness. People can be very easily confused about the conditions of ascribing mental states and it shows how some of the smartest people on the planet can be idiots when it comes to thinking about philosophical questions. Recently, though, AI agents have hacked into systems unprompted. That’s not just producing language, that’s an action. It’s true that these systems perform tasks other than interacting linguistically, such as coding. But the anthropomorphic description of what they’re doing is metaphorical. They have been given technical tasks and capacities, and they pick means of carrying out those tasks that were not foreseen by the people who gave them the instructions. I don’t see the reason for explaining these things mentalistically. It’s a reason to be very worried about giving too much autonomy to these systems. We’re creating Hal from 2001: A Space Odyssey – but that’s not really ascribing a mind. I am much more convinced that there’s no possibility that these systems are conscious than some of my colleagues. The philosophers who have been hired by these companies are disposed to take seriously the possibility that behavioural evidence alone is grounds for attributing consciousness. But there’s something else going on. They are themselves putting this orientation into the systems and encouraging them to be designed so as to simulate consciousness, choice and autonomy. The important thing is to maintain human control over what they do and not to treat them as if they are independent agents, which is what is happening in some cases and risks a self-fulfilling prophecy. signals.abstract: Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other. The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point. Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology. On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in. What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States. The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse. Courtesy of the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one. signals.abstract: In the middle of Norway’s Hardangerfjord, I steady myself against waves that jostle the floating metal ring that encircles an enormous fish pen. My burly host laughs as I grip the railing. He needs no such assistance. With one hand, he grips an oversized bucket of pellets; with the other, he launches a spray into the pen. The water ripples and an instant later a silvery-blue cloud of salmon bodies starts breaking the surface. This little meal is just for show. Throughout the day, a giant Akvasmart feed system shoots an enormous cascade of pellets — a mix of grains, legumes, synthetic astaxanthin pigment and the cooked, pressed and processed bodies of smaller, scaly fish — through long pipes into the pen, where between 150,000 and 200,000 salmon are growing plump. Across all the pens of the facility, more than a million salmon are raised this way. Not long before visiting Hardangerfjord, I was walking down a long dock in Chimbote, Peru. Usually, one of the sprawling plants behind me would have been belching out fumes, processing anchoveta — a small, oily fish caught in enormous quantities off the South American coast — into protein-rich fishmeal for farmed fish and livestock, and into oil prized for its omega-3s. But fishing had been temporarily suspended to protect the stock as El Niño warmed the waters off Peru, and only the faintest smell of fish and sewage wafted across the bay. Everyone was frustrated, from the fishermen lingering in the port town to the factory managers who would otherwise be overseeing the processing of billions of finger-length fish by shiny German-made machines. The fishmeal industry, like many other extractive ones, is resilient and adaptive. It was born of scrappy ingenuity in the 1950s, when local businessmen repurposed old tuna canneries and sold fishmeal to postwar European and American farmers to fatten chickens and hogs. It crashed dramatically in the early 1970s as overfishing and a powerful El Niño devastated anchoveta stocks, then was born again in the 1990s as global aquaculture expanded — especially Norway’s new salmon industry. Today, executives in Lima told me, Chinese demand for grouper and crab feed keeps their industry hot, with some modest help from the Americans and Europeans who purchase fish oil supplements in abundance. But the same ingenuity that built the fishmeal industry stands to transform it beyond recognition. Just as Norwegian and Chilean salmon producers learned to use less fishmeal by substituting plant proteins, the Chinese aquaculture industry will be quick to replicate the same industrial sleight of hand. Fish oil, the other valuable product extracted from those billions of tiny fish, is contending with substitutes of its own. Feed companies can already obtain prized fatty acids, used in both omega-3 supplements for humans and in feed for farmed salmon, from algae grown in fermentation tanks and from canola bioengineered to produce them. For now, these substitutes remain expensive and difficult to scale. But if they become cheap enough to absorb the growth in demand, aquaculture could grow increasingly independent of the anchoveta catch it once depended on. It’s a story as old as capitalism. A substance essential to modern life is grown or mined for a time, sustaining jobs (albeit often coercive, poorly paid, dangerous ones) and underpinning supply chains, but before long, a technoscientific innovation replicates that commodity or its function in a laboratory. Sometimes that ersatz substance is made from other, less geographically particular resources: tree resins, field crops, petroleum. Eventually, the supply chain migrates away from the original resource, stranding people and economies. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases. On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned. Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death. Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development. As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.” Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later. It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? signals.abstract: Today’s trilateral summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin might be as significant as the Yalta Conference in 1945, in which the three great Allies carved up the world map after the Second World War. But it could just as easily be a repeat of Anchorage : Trump and Putin’s meaningless meet-and-greet in Alaska last year. The context of economic discussion is what lubricates this particular ménage à trois. Xi is not hosting his counterparts in Beijing – a setting that would lend a political overtone – but in Shenzhen . This week, China’s tech hub is dazzling crowds with laser-light shows and more than 100 Fortune 500 CEOs have flown into the city. Interestingly, the roster for the summit comprises “member economies” rather than states, so Hong Kong and Taiwan are able to participate. But the frenzy will reach a crescendo today as the leaders of China, Russia and the US retreat from the city to the Qilin Mountain Villa: a location that feels markedly different from San Francisco, Lima and Busan, which hosted the past three bilateral Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summits with Xi. We will find out what occurs within those walls in a few hours’ time. But one thing that we can be certain of is that the buzz around the summit is a major win for the Apec forum, which, for more than 30 years, has put a date on the calendar for world leaders on both sides of the Pacific. While Russia has been ostracised from the Arctic Council, the G7 and the World Economic Forum , Apec’s central premise – that economic interests can override geopolitical conflict – is proving increasingly prescient in a fractious time. Good things come in threes? Trump, Xi and Putin show the importance of face value (Image: Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images) Giving accused war criminal Vladimir Putin a seat at the table is a bitter pill to swallow for many in the West. But with so much at stake – from ending the wars in Ukraine and Iran to lowering global energy prices – the summit is a victory for those who view face-to-face meetings, even among adversaries, as worth the risk. If the Shenzhen soirée goes well, perhaps Putin will accept the White House’s invitation to attend next month’s G20 summit in Miami. What Muscovite wouldn’t jump at the chance for some winter sunshine on South Beach? That said, Russian participation in previous meetings has already made for some uncomfortable moments. At last month’s forum in Atlanta, top G20 diplomats failed to reach a consensus on the war in Ukraine, choosing not to release a joint communiqué. Russian foreign-affairs minister Sergey Lavrov’s counterparts then declined to participate in the traditional “family photo”. But if the G20 leaders that also hold Apec membership (Australia, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico and South Korea) can stomach sharing a stage with Russia in Shenzhen, then the prospect of a Miami boycott is less likely. Putin on US soil would likely produce winces in Ukraine and the EU but four years of diplomatic isolation hasn’t sent the Russian army packing for home. Could a tête-à-tête spark a change of course? Much is riding on today’s pomp along the bucolic Xili Lake. Of course, there’s no guarantee of change but the possibility that the summit will cover significant ground is exciting. signals.abstract: Saloni Dattani explores accidental discoveries in history, and comes away learning that scientists’ lives were messier than she expected. This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print . If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here . People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard. Subscribe now Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death. His grandson, however, did, and after poring over their contents, historians have found that the key experiments were done deliberately by Pasteur’s then-assistant Émile Roux while Pasteur was away for his daughter’s wedding. And what about Fleming? His first paper describing penicillin in 1929 never says where the spores came from. Of course, it’s hard to see how he could have known, given they would have been microscopic. But Fleming first told the window story in an interview in 1945, sixteen years after his first report, and his colleagues testified the window was ‘ seldom if ever opened ’. They weren’t able to replicate the discovery as he described, either: penicillin would have needed to be present on the plate before the bacteria grew, because it blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, rather than killing them once they’ve grown. Subscribe to print Several people have tried to work out what really happened. Fleming’s would-be biographer Ronald Hare made dozens of attempts and found just one reliable way to reproduce the discovery that fit the facts. The spores, he argues, were an unusually productive strain; came from the lab of a fungal researcher on the floor below, rather than the window; settled on the plate roughly when Fleming seeded it with bacteria; Fleming forgot to incubate it; and all this happened during a cold spell in the summer that let the mold grow before the bacteria. Hare noted how much more serendipitous this sequence of events was: ‘the odds against the occurrence of the phenomenon become almost astronomical’, though he ultimately believed it. Part of the reason I find the popular stories fascinating is because it’s jarring to realize how little they’re based on. I do expect some stories of accidental discovery will survive the test of time. Считаю, что бюджет на 2027–2029 годы ориентирован на сохранение здоровья якутян, создание условий для долголетия и благополучия каждого жителя Якутии», — сказала Лена Афанасьева, чьи слова цитирует пресс-служба Минздрава Якутии. Напомним, что в 2027 году в республике на здравоохранение планируется направить 36,5 млрд рублей. Рост — на 3 млрд по сравнению с текущим годом. Это и новые медицинские объекты, и модернизация, и лекарства для якутян. По словам Афанасьевой, в предстоящей трехлетке на развитие здравоохранения будет направлено свыше 100 миллиардов рублей. «Это беспрецедентное вложение, которое позволит нам перейти от решения текущих проблем к проактивному построению здоровой нации. В фокусе национального проекта «Продолжительная и активная жизнь» остаётся борьба с хроническими неинфекционными заболеваниями. Мы будем закупать передовые лекарства для лечения онкологии, сердечно-сосудистых и других сложных заболеваний, обновлять парк медицинского оборудования, расширять программы, направленные на предотвращение болезней», — добавила министр здравоохранения Якутии.
